speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the deadlock that now exists in respect of the international treaty for Columbia river development.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I have before me a motion by the Leader of the Opposition for the adjournment of the house under standing order 26. One has to consider in these matters whether they are of urgent national importance and also the question of urgency of debate at this particular time. It is on that particular point that I have some doubts, and I am quite prepared to hear the Leader of the Opposition in regard to urgency of debate at this particular time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have, of course, very rightly called attention to the consideration of urgency in moving a motion of this kind, a consideration which, as you have already indicated on other occasions, cannot be entirely divorced from the consideration of national importance. I take it there is no division of opinion over the question of the national importance of this matter and the deadlock in respect of this treaty, the consequences of which are of such far reaching significance to our country. Also, Mr. Speaker, bearing on the questions of urgency and importance is the fact that in a series of answers in the house and statements made outside the house in my view, confusion has been created. Moreover the impasse that we find ourselves in with regard to this matter affects both national interests and those of our relations with the United States.
Now, Mr. Speaker, on the immediate question of urgency as related to these developments I have mentioned, the chief negotiator of the treaty on behalf of Canada, the present Minister of Public Works, has already discussed this matter outside the house. In the course of those discussions, and in a letter 27507-3-154J
which he has written to the editor of a magazine entitled Engineering and Contract Record, the Minister of Public Works emphasizes that debate on this matter should be in parliament. In this letter of September 17, 1962 he said, and quite rightly:
I feel that the proper forum for such detailed comment is the prospective hearing in parliament. X am sure that it will he desired to investigate every aspect of the treaty and obtain the views of all persons concerned with it. I should myself appear in such a case . .
We regret, of course, that the Minister of Public Works has decided to leave us, and if he is to participate in a discussion of this important matter that discussion must take place at once while he has an opportunity to do so. If the committee on external affairs, which is the committee to which this matter would be submitted, were set up; if the government could give us the assurance that the committee would be set up immediately so the matter could be referred to it, then of course I would be glad to withdraw this motion so that the discussion could take place at once with the Minister of Public Works, other ministers and other persons concerned present. However, unless there is some assurance that this can be done, then I very respectfully submit this motion to you for consideration. Since the Minister of Public Works will be leaving us so shortly, it is a matter of great urgency to have this matter discussed at once and in his presence.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition establish anything it is that this is not a definite matter of urgent public importance. In the first place it is not, as described in the motion, a definite matter at all. The Leader of the Opposition talked about a deadlock that he says now exists in respect of an international treaty with regard to the Columbia river development. I have some familiarity with the situation in general in respect of the Columbia river, and I do not know what he is talking about. There is no deadlock.

Columbia River Treaty point, I think it would be helpful to the Chair if we stayed on that point. We will continue.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition are to be stripped down to what he had to say as to the urgency of debate there will not be very much left in his remarks. What has he got? He talked about the subject in general, but negotiations and discussions are proceeding. There has been no finality reached on this at all and discussion has been proceeding for some time.

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

On such motions, Mr. Speaker, my remarks relate to submissions to you and what I am saying is pitched to a level to meet the requirement that you have in mind and not just an appeal to the intelligence or lesser intelligence of some hon. members opposite who are stronger on noise than they are on understanding.
I repeat that when there is talk about a deadlock now existing in respect to this international treaty for the Columbia river development, I say there is no deadlock. There is today what has been going on continually, a series of discussions which are not complete. There is no urgency of debate in this respect today unless there was urgency of debate in respect to it a month ago, two months, three months or six months ago, because we are dealing with a continuing situation in which talks are continuing and plans exist for a continuance of talks at the governmental level. To talk about urgency of debate about this matter at the moment, where no definite matter of urgent public importance is concerned, is simply absurd.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether you heard the uproarious and most unintelligent remark of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

I am only concerned about argument which would support the question of urgency of debate at this moment. The Chair is prepared to hear brief argument in this regard, and I say "brief" because the Chair has already pretty well made up its mind on the representations which have been made on both sides in respect to this matter. I shall hear further argument if hon. members wish to put forward a point briefly as to the necessity of debate this morning.
[Mr. Speaker.)

subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in answer to several questions which I have posed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the house has learned that discussions are about to be resumed with respect to the sale of downstream benefits in the United States; that is respecting the duration, price and so on with regard to that sale. Article VIII of the treaty specifically states that the price and other terms and conditions of this sale are to be determined after ratification of the treaty and not beforehand. It would be most helpful to the house if the government could explain the purpose of the present negotiations and discussions between Canada and the United States; also if article VIII of the treaty is to be binding on both countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member for Coast-Capilano has mentioned me in his remarks I think it should be made clear that on one or probably two occasions last week, or it may have been a few days earlier than that, I explained in answer to questions that there had been two informal meetings at which representatives of the Canadian government, the United States government and the government of British Columbia had been present. I said these were informal meetings and were certainly not for the purpose of negotiating price for downstream benefits, as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano has intimated today. He goes much further than the statement I made, and I also pointed out that there were to be further talks later this month on, I believe, December 19 and 20.
Since we are in the midst of these talks, in which a foreign government is concerned, how can there possibly be any basis for the charge that the Leader of the Opposition makes today, which is that there has been a deadlock? I submit it would be entirely contrary to the rules were the house to go on and spend a day discussing this matter about which there are to be talks in less than two weeks.

We have suggested an alternative, that is that this matter be referred to a committee of the house, which could very well be set up at this moment, and not necessarily for the purpose of ratifying the agreement.
When the Prime Minister returned from Washington on January 18, 1961 he was asked whether this matter should go before a committee of the house for discussion prior to final agreement with British Columbia. The Prime Minister implied that this was not necessary, that it could be discussed here. The terms of this agreement can and may be discussed here without necessarily meaning ratification.

speechtext: I am submitting, Mr. Speaker, that a matter which has been in abeyance for almost two years is urgent and should be clarified; that some public discussion should be held so the country and this parliament can understand what is the government's intention and what project the government has in mind. Mr. Speaker, I intend to relate my very short remarks to the matter of urgency only. A number of questions on this matter have been replied to in this house, one of them by the Minister of Public Works on November 30, when he stated:
We have maintained in general the policy which we had and which we felt to be the correct one. Sincere efforts have been made, however, to see whether it is possible to find a meeting ground between the two positions which had thus come into conflict, in order that this great project might be commenced at the earliest possible date. It has been difficult, but those discussions are still going on.
I suggest to you, sir, that this indicates a matter of extreme difficulty and great conflict, and therefore urgency, and we should know what the differences are between the various positions.

Order. I am quite satisfied that this motion does not meet the requirements of standing order 26. If we refer to citation 100 in Beauchesne we see a number of reasons why this is so.

Columbia River Treaty
First of all, it must be a matter of recent occurrence, of immediate recent occurrence. If there has been a difference of opinion with regard to this particular question, as hon. members have indicated in their remarks, this may have existed for some considerable time. Certainly it existed at a time when this matter could have been raised in this house in weeks past. Certainly it was adverted to in the debate on the speech from the throne, when this formed the subject of remarks by a number of hon. members.
With regard to the other point that the Minister of Public Works allegedly was leaving this house, the Chair is not aware of that event happening next week, or the week after, or when it might happen. Therefore in the estimation of the Chair that does not found a ground for adjourning the business under standing order 26. For these reasons I find the motion unacceptable.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monfeifh (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON DRUGS AND CHEMICAL FOOD CONTAMINATION
speechtext:
That a special committee be appointed to consider and report upon (a) the law and practices relating to the control of the introduction, marketing and use of drugs: and (b) the dangers arising from contamination of food by the use of chemicals to kill weeds, insects and other pests;
2428	HOUSE OF
Establishment of Committee on Drugs
That the committee consist of 15 members to he designated by the house;
That the committee be empowered to send for persons and papers and to report from time to time;
That the committee be empowered to sit during the sittings of the house;
That the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable; and
That standing order 66 be suspended in relation thereto.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that on November 30 I indicated the government's intention to recommend the establishment of a special committee to consider and report upon certain aspects of the food and drug responsibilities of my department. In consequence a government notice of motion appeared on Votes and Proceedings of Friday, November 30, and was transferred to government orders on December 3. This resolution is set out on today's order paper, Mr. Speaker.
I do not believe I need to read it into the record at this stage. I do not believe I need to dwell on the reasons for this motion which will, I am sure, be supported by all hon. members. Events over the past year, and indeed in recent months almost on a daily basis, have clearly indicated the uncertainties which we are facing in the drug field. While the matter of the contamination of food by the use of chemicals designed to kill weeds, insects and other pests has perhaps not yet gained as high a degree of public attention, it does represent a problem which is likely to become more and more prominent in the years ahead.
As the house is aware, our new drug procedures have been under intensive study by a special committee of the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons. The report of its findings, together with recommendations, is nearing completion and should be available for consideration by the proposed parliamentary committee. There is also the matter of Bill No. C-3, which has initiated several fundamental changes in our food and drug legislation. In my opinion these changes represent a very real advance in providing some degree of control over the distribution of drug samples and in strengthening our authority in respect of the introduction and withdrawal of drugs.
However, I also felt that it would be well for hon. members to have an opportunity to consider not only the legislation itself but also the practices and procedures relating to control of the introduction, marketing and use of drugs. In the judgment of the government the most effective way of accomplishing this kind of broad and detailed study would be through the establishment of a special


committee with such a composition and terms of reference as are set out in the motion now before the house.
I know that all hon. members will join with me, Mr. Speaker, in paying tribute to the effective job which has been done within the authority of the Food and Drugs Act. The fact that we are now giving thought to an investigation of the important parts of this structure is in no way a reflection on the record achieved over the years. However, we seem to be moving into a new era, not only of widening opportunity but also of great complexity in the food and drug field. I think we have a public responsibility to take every possible step to ensure that our legislation and procedures are geared, in so far as is humanly possible, to these new and changing circumstances. I might say that while the work of the committee is going on, the food and drug directorate and other research institutions as well as the drug companies themselves are pushing forward with their research on drug testing. Any information we obtain that would be helpful to the medical profession will be passed on to them promptly. Surely, Mr. Speaker, a lesson to be learned from the recent tragedy is that pregnant women should only take drugs on the advice of their physicians.
In presenting this resolution to the house I ask for the support of all hon. members in approving it so the matter may be carried out without further delay.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON DRUGS AND CHEMICAL FOOD CONTAMINATION

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON DRUGS AND CHEMICAL FOOD CONTAMINATION
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, has this anything to do with the resolution before us?

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON DRUGS AND CHEMICAL FOOD CONTAMINATION
speechtext: It certainly has.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMITTEE ON DRUGS AND CHEMICAL FOOD CONTAMINATION
speechtext:
When it does try to legislate it brings in half baked, incomplete, and incoherent legislation or proposals with which to patch up existing laws. These are often mere palliatives where radical surgery is most urgently needed, and it is no wonder, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada have rejected this government and are demanding a change. This resolution is another example of long overdue and incomplete proposals. We are faced in this committee with an assignment of a serious nature, in an area of supreme importance to the health and life of the Canadian people.
It has already been stated, both by the minister and others in this house and in the other place, that Canada's Food and Drugs Act of 1953 is second to none in the world and that it was regarded as a model by the world health organization and many countries which used it as the basis for their own drug and food legislation. I am happy to hear this praise, for it gives credit to the former minister of health, an illustrious member of this house, who has served and continues to serve this house, devoting all his years and all his talents to the common good of all in this country.
Mr. Speaker, in this period of rapidly advancing technological progress in the field of chemistry, the industrialized world is confronted with far reaching changes and progress in foods, drugs, cosmetics and pesticides. In order to keep up with this scientific progress, responsible governments must update their legislation and regulations, thus discharging their responsibility for scientific progress as well as for public safety. That is why we should regularly review vital legislation pertaining to health and life. It is unfortunate that the thalidomide tragedy, producing so many malformed infants and giving their parents untold grief, has forced this and other governments to pay more attention and to initiate a probe into the matter of drugs. I believe that public protection is the overriding motive in considering this probe and new legislation. While government, industry, the medical profession and the consumer have their responsibilities, all of us in this house have the grave responsibility to probe into this matter and enact the best possible legislation for the good of all concerned.
Establishment of Committee on Drugs
Much has been said and written about the thalidomide tragedy in Canada. Many Canadians have been asking why this misfortune happened in Canada but was avoided in the United States of America. Many Canadians are still asking for the complete explanation of why this government waited three months to request the withdrawal of thalidomide from the Canadian market when Germany did so on November 26, 1961, and Canada waited until March 2, 1962. Many Canadians are alarmed at the removal of many drugs from the market which were previously approved as safe and effective by the food and drug directorate. Many Canadians are increasingly succumbing to iatrogenic or drug-induced diseases and drug allergies. Many patients are revolting against the high cost of drugs. Pharmacists and doctors are complaining about the confusion of the multiplicity of drugs, many of which are ineffective and others dangerous. Responsible laymen and doctors are complaining about the deluge of flamboyant and even misleading advertising of drugs on television, radio, press and in mailed literature.
North Americans, Mr. Speaker, have been stunned by the revelations about chemical pesticides written by a scientist and marine biologist, Miss Rachel Carson, in a book entitled "Silent Spring". In this document we find an indictment of the indiscriminate use of new chemicals which are contaminating our food and our whole environment. This should warn us to be careful, and to prod governments to review their legislation to ensure the safety of the public and the survival of nature.
Besides this government's slowness in banning thalidomide, it has introduced both confusion and dismay in medical research centres by prohibiting the further distribution of lysergic acid diethylamide. Many of us have received complaints from researchers in psychiatry and alcoholism protesting the banning of L.S.D. This drug has been found to be very promising for use in "depth" psychotherapy. Apparently there is no evidence of serious danger if the drug is used by competent psychiatrists who employ full security precautions during the period of its effectiveness. These researchers ask that they should be permitted to work with it in their research projects both in psychiatry and alcoholism. Specialists at the Ontario alcoholism research foundation have recently embarked on a research study of L.S.D., believing that it may be a valuable treatment for alcoholics. Dr. F. S. Lawson, director of the Saskatchewan psychiatric services, claims that L.S.D. had given 50 per cent improvement rate in alcoholics when other treatments failed.

Establishment of Committee on Drugs
As yet the government has not decided to give these researchers a clear directive and immediate notice concerning the future availability of L.S.D. The world is filled with so many intensely dangerous chemicals that it seems utterly stupid to ban a few which happen to be suitable for use as drugs. It would be tragically unfair to restrict the availability of L.S.D. now that medical researchers have learned to use it properly. What could be done in this case is for the health department to decide to what research institutions L.S.D. should be made available, and to demand that a record be kept of each occasion on which the drug is used, with accounting of all stocks available for inspection at any time. I hope the government will quickly notify these researchers of its final decision.
There are other aspects of the Food and Drugs Act which neither the amendments nor the preliminary remarks of the minister have explained, aspects and problems which are important and today call for stronger legislation. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization last summer issued a warning against the use of additives in baby foods. Other problems consist of drug nomenclature, the proper testing of drugs for teratogenicity, the licensing of all drug manufacturers and distributors, ethical advertising both to the medical profession and to lay people, and closer scrutiny of food additives, cosmetics and chemical pesticides.
The public and the medical profession have become uneasy and deeply concerned with the abuses that exist today and keep on increasing in the fields of medical advertising, various food additives, potent pesticides, cosmetics and certain drugs. People are easy marks for ineffective medicine, and there is a danger there of self-medication. The Canadian people are also incensed and indignant at the very high cost of drugs today. I believe that part of this high cost is due to the expensive and, alas, flamboyant advertising both to doctors in their journals and to the public. Just the other day the director of the food and drug directorate expressed his fears about the way advertisers are finding ways to evade advertising regulations.
Another grave problem in this field is the multiplicity of drugs available today. The chief pharmacist of St. Joseph's hospital in Hamilton stressed only about three weeks ago at the Ontario hospital association convention the confusion which exists both in the pharmacies and on the floors of hospitals in view of the multiplicity of drugs. I believe, therefore, that a close examination of this matter is urgent.
Mr. Speaker, let me remind the minister at this point that Dr. Helen Taussig of Johns

Hopkins University, who did a thorough study of phocomelia, was greatly impressed with photographs of unborn rats with defects of the extremities produced by the ingestion of thalidomide. That is why she suggested that all new drugs which circulate through the bloodstream should be screened for their effect on the offspring of several species of pregnant animals. There are already several drugs in medical use that are known today to be teratogenic in animals. A few drugs, aminopterin, estrogens, androgens, progestins and thalidomide are known to be teratogenic in man as well as in animals. There is need, therefore, for a program in which all drugs given to a population of pregnant women may be recorded and the offspring followed up for many years. But it would be most prudent, according to leading obstetricians in this country, that medication should not be given to pregnant women without very definite medical indications. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of National Health and Welfare should instruct the members of the medical profession to follow this wise advice.
All these extensive tests and controls by qualified investigators mean more work and more expense. This means more highly qualified personnel and more adequate laboratories. It is disappointing that in an answer to a question I asked a few years ago it was stated that there are still about 30 positions in the food and drug directorate which have been vacant for many months. There are many problems in the marketing of safe and effective drugs. On October 4, 1962 the 87th congress of the United States of America unanimously passed many amendments to their food and drug act. These amendments were the result of an exhaustive two year study by a special congressional committee, which also probed the relationship of patent laws with regard to high drug prices.
We in this house welcome the opportunity to study this whole problem with the help of expert advice. But we should remember that all the recommendations and all the additional powers that may be granted to the food and drug directorate, much as they should do to prevent a repetition of the thalidomide tragedy, will not absolutely banish the hazards associated with the use of drugs. Should the future show inadequacies in the laws now being passed, let us hope the pattern of progress will not be repeated again through catastrophe.
Mr. Speaker, with regard to the specific points of reference of this resolution, let me point out to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that they are completely inadequate. There is no mention, for example, of any scrutiny of the problem of cosmetics yet

this problem has been scrutinized by the special committee of the United States congress and it was proved that a great deal of danger has occurred to women by the use of cosmetic sprays. When the house is considering a motion, of which notice has been given, for the appointment of a select committee, a member cannot move an amendment that the committee be given wider powers than those which were set down in the notice.

This is a question on which I spoke when the original motion came up and it was not my intention to spend more than five or ten minutes discussing it now because, in my opinion, the facts are so clear that

Establishment of Committee on Drugs they do not need to be gone into at any great length. But, if hon. members on this side of the house insist on interrupting I shall certainly have to take the time to go into more detail than would ordinarily be necessary. I wonder if the hon. member who interjected has had occasion or the interest to look at the report prepared by Mr. Henry, the director of investigation and research, Combines Investigation Act. If he looks at it and reads the conclusions he will understand what I mean. I want to read just a couple of paragraphs which I am sure will convince any member of this house who is open to reason that this is a question which not only could be, but must be discussed in the committee when it meets. I quote, Mr. Speaker, from page 257.
The information obtained in this inquiry appears to indicate that, at the manufacturers level, prices of certain drugs are affected by the control over the manufacture, distribution and sale of such drugs exercised through patents. The provisions of the Patent Act relating to compulsory licences appear to have proved ineffectual to combat this situation and the clear intent of the act has been frustrated. This conclusion is not intended to imply any opinion about patents as such, it is intended simply to indicate that, in relation to the sale of drugs in Canada, patents have been and are being used to create monopolistic situations which the Canadian law appears to have been designed to prevent. The control exercised over the manufacture, distribution and sale of certain drugs through patents has virtually eliminated price competition in respect of such drugs and has encouraged other forms of competition which, while possibly bringing other benefits to the public, have resulted in prices being increased rather than decreased.
Further on Mr. Henry says:
Prices of drugs in Canada are among the highest in the world. These prices tend to reflect current prices of the same or comparative drug products in the United States but, because of the sales tax applicable in Canada, prices to consumers in Canada are about 11 per cent higher.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest to hon. members that this is a clear indication of the importance of discussing the question. If hon. members are still in doubt, I would suggest that they look at the findings of the Kefauver committee in the United States. Let me quote just a couple of lines from Senator Kefauver's report. Hon. members will find this in report No. 448 at page 50:
Using the average stockholders' equity at the beginning and end of 1959 as the denominator, and the profits for the year as the numerator, the rate of return for the drug industry... was 18.1 per cent. In contrast, the average rate for all manufacturing corporations was 10.5 per cent. In terms of profits as per cent of sales, the drug industry averaged 10.3 per cent whereas all manufacturing corporations averaged 4.8 per cent.
Then Senator Kefauver goes on to point out how on particular drugs, such as one of the most popular tranquilizers, one of the large companies was making over one and
[Mr. Orlikow.l
a half cents profit on every single tablet they sold to the American public in millions, if not billions, every year. When we see this situation it is not at all surprising that in the opinion of members of this group it is of the utmost importance that the problem of drug prices should be gone into thoroughly by the committee. I am sure that whichever of our members are on that committee they will make this one of the first proposals to the committee when it meets.
I would like to say just a few words about some of the other matters which have been dealt, with up to now. I was amazed, I must say, by the speech we heard this morning from the hon. member from Parkdale, Mr. Haidasz, because most of the things of which he accused this government, their indecision, their failure to act, and so on, the difficulties he pointed out, the problems which have arisen in connection with the sale of cosmetics, the irritating chemicals which have been found in cosmetics, the problems he raised in connection with all the other drugs which he mentioned and the problems in connection with pesticides, have been with us for many years, and were problems which were with us even when the former government was in office. I do not say this is an excuse for this government not having acted, but why the hon. member for Parkdale got so excited, I find it difficult to understand. Surely the one thing that has come out of the evidence with regard to the difficulties which have arisen from the drug thalidomide is the fact that the law was not strong enough, not tight enough to give the department the authority to order the discontinuance of the use of the drug. The department had only advisory power; it had to work in cooperation with the drug companies, and so naturally the department was loath, I am sure, to act until it was 100 per cent certain it was correct.
It seems to me that one of the things the committee will have to do will be to make inquiries as to what procedures would be best, so that the department will have the flexibility and yet the right and authority to call for the discontinuance or the suspension of the use of a drug if and when it is found that the drug is harmful.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, and having said on an earlier occasion that I thought the government moved much too slowly in the thalidomide case, from everything I can And out the department is moving much too fast in connection with the banning of the L.S.D. drug. The leader of this group mentioned this morning that a hospital in North Battleford was told that they could not get

their usual supply of L.S.D. This matter was taken up with the minister and it is true that steps have been taken to correct the situation. I think this is the important point, however, which the committee will have to look into, not only because of the importance of L.S.D. but because the procedures go to the whole heart of how we should deal with drugs in this rapidly changing situation, when there are new drugs almost every day. The fact is that as far as I can find out the provision in the bill to prohibit the use of L.S.D. was made without consultation with the people who have been using it. As far as I can find out, the drug has been used in only a very few institutions and under the most rigid control, and yet in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec, the decision to ban the use of the drug was taken without consultation with the people concerned.
In an order for return which was tabled the other day, in the correspondence dealing with this subject there appears a letter dated October 18, 1962, to Dr. J. D. Murphy, chief medical officer of the food and drug directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare in Ottawa. The letter is from Dr. Hoffer, the director of psychiatric research in the province of Saskatchewan and reads as follows:
Dear Dr. Murphy:
I have just seen a circular sent by Dr. Morrell, dated October 12, 1962, in which thalidomide and lysergic acid diethylamide are placed on the schedule H. Does this mean that L.S.D. will no longer be available for clinical use? As you know, we have now treated perhaps 500 alcoholics in this province, and we would be very annoyed indeed if we could no longer get access to it. Would you please let me know immediately.
That is signed by Dr. Hoffer. The fact that the people in Saskatchewan have now been informed that they can get it is, I think, good; but the fact that they were not consulted in the decision that was made indicates a very serious defect in the whole set-up. I have a letter dated November 11, 1962, from Dr. D. Ewen Cameron of the Allan Memorial Institute. Dr. Cameron is at present the president of the world psychiatric association. The letter is written to me in response to a letter on my part asking about this question. I would like to read into the record, Mr. Speaker, what Dr. Cameron says. Of course, the letter is available to the minister if he would like to see it. It says:
Frankly, many of us have been somewhat concerned over the reaction to the thalidomide tragedy. There has seemed to be a danger that in dealing with this particular matter we may set up such stringent regulations that the progress of medical research may be substantially slowed. It is a matter of common knowledge that when ether and chloroform were first introduced and, indeed, when the early drugs for the control of syphilis
Establishment of Committee on Drugs were produced, deaths occurred which were attributable to the therapeutic agents themselves. This was also true, at least in the early days, of insulin and yet, even in retrospect, would anyone willingly take the position that chloroform and ether should not have been introduced when they were, or that the use of insulin should have been deferred for another 30 years until we had the present, much safer, oral forms of administration?
It seems to me that there is little progress anywhere in human affairs without some price being paid. This is apparent in the progress we have made in transportation by the development of the automobile and yet I think no one anticipates that we will eventually travel to the planets without some men's lives being lost on the way.
In my own field, insulin coma treatment regularly killed a certain percentage of patients every year and so did the malarial treatment of general paresis. Yet so serious were the diseases that no one at any time urged that these should be abandoned until they had, as we do now, still better and safer methods. Indeed, if we stepped back from the matter, we must agree that the whole business of living is a calculated risk.
Turning, however, to the practical issues, I am sorry that L.S.D. has been picked out for special attention. We have used it for many years. It is quite a harmless preparation. It is useful for diagnostic purposes, particularly for the obtaining of information which can subsequently be applied in psychotherapy. Some people have found it of value psychotherapeutically, but our interest and use of it has been, as I say, chiefly diagnostic. However, apart from any particular drug, my great hope is that whatever regulations are set up, they will not be too burdensome and time-consuming, for if they slow down the processes of research we can be quite sure that many, many more will be harassed and crippled or even die, than will be protected.
This letter clearly indicates that we are in a difficult field. There are no easy answers. One cannot say in advance what drugs should be banned and what drugs should be permitted. It is my hope that the committee will call as witnesses not only representatives of the drug industry but representatives of the medical colleges, of the clinics, of the practising physicians and others who can testify as to the experiments they are making and the results they have found. Otherwise, we shall find it impossible to devise practical methods of control. Yet control there must be. I think it would have been much better if the provisions of the bill the government lately brought in had been sent to the committee for consideration along with the other matters. I hope that when this committee meets it will take the widest latitude to call all witnesses who might be in a position to give it expert advice.
I do not want to get into a debate about whether this is a good act now, or whether it was a good act ten years ago, but I might point out that there are thousands of preparations being put on the market every year not only in connection with medicine but with agriculture and forestry. In my opinion proper protection for the people of

Mr. Speaker, I want to nibble on this well known parliamentary bone for a few minutes because I am particularly interested in one aspect of this resolution. Like the rest of the members of this party, I support the resolution wholeheartedly and I consider that the work of this committee, if it is given sufficient scope, will be of greater importance to the Canadian people than the setting up of the economic development council.
I trust that when the committee deals with the question of the control, marketing and use of drugs it will call witnesses from the drug industry, the medical professions, from the trade and also from the department. I think the committee should be given ample time in which to make as full an investigation as possible of all aspects of this question. I think the word "marketing" in the terms of reference is an unfortunate one. In my opinion it would have been much better if the resolution has used the word "distribution" because then there would have been no doubt about the cost of drugs being within the field of inquiry. I hope the committee does have full power to obtain evidence as to the cost of drugs because this represents an important question to many Canadians.


I was talking to my hon. friend who has just resumed his seat and he has numerous cases where people for whom certain prescriptions had been written could not take advantage of those prescriptions because they could not afford to buy the drugs. One person in Ottawa some months ago gave me a pathetic illustration of that situation. I hope the committee will call before it representatives of the manufacturers, of the trade and of the retailers in connection with the cost of drugs. I understand that usually the retailers are blamed for the high cost of drugs because they come into direct contact with the consumer. However, their prices are largely determined by the prices charged by the manufacturers.
Then, under (b), the resolution gives the committee power to consider and report on the dangers arising from the contamination of food by the use of chemicals to kill weeds, insects and other pests. I have been interested in this aspect of the question for some years. I am, of course, very interested in agriculture and I see both sides of the question-the point of view of the agriculturist and also the approach of the person concerned with the preservation of human and wildlife. I am not sure whether this resolution covers an investigation of the damage done by these chemicals on the health of wildlife.
Considerable damage has been caused to the health of wildlife in this country as a result of the use of insecticides and pesticides. I am not sure whether I am in order in mentioning that matter, Mr. Speaker, I see you looking at me with some doubt. I therefore shall not go along that route any further except to say that I am one of those who, when it comes to a question of sacrificing certain land that could be drained in order to preserve a duck habitat or landing area, I will save the place for the ducks rather than bring into production the land in question.
Since you have indicated, Mr. Speaker, that you do not like me to trespass on the rules I am not going to quote from a document which I have here and which was written by an important person who is very much interested in this problem. However, when it comes to the question of the effect of the dangers arising from contamination of food by the use of chemicals to kill weeds, insects and other pests, I consider the committee has there a very heavy task and one that is not going to be completed in a few weeks.
I suggest that this is a problem of such great urgency and of such great importance that witnesses will have to be called, particularly persons who have conducted research into this type of thing. I should like to see

called before the committee representatives of agriculture organizations; representatives of the trade, that is to say manufacturers and distributors of these products; and representatives of the consumers organizations of Canada. They have been quite interested in this problem for a number of years from a consumers point of view. I think that the Consumers Association of Canada and other similar organizations should have an opportunity to express their views before this committee. Then I should like to see officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare called before the committee in order to get their side of the story and also officials of the Department of Agriculture, particularly the gentlemen who recently, I thought rather hurriedly and rather caustically, criticized the book recently published by Rachel Carson, entitled "Silent Spring". I consider that an examination of this question will require the calling of witnesses from very wide fields.
In connection with this subject I wish to draw to the attention of the house this book, "Silent Spring" written by Rachel Carson. I suggest that any member of this committee and any member of parliament who is interested in the health of the nation and in the health of our wildlife should purchase this book. I purchased it recently and found it to be most informative and most enlightening, and I have followed this subject for many years. In support of my argument with regard to the necessity for full consideration of this aspect of the resolution-and I am rising to speak particularly because of this aspect of the resolution-I wish to quote briefly from this book in order to rouse hon. members' interest in the book itself and in the subject.
At page 15 of this book, commencing with chapter 3 entitled, "Elixirs of Death", the writer states as follows:
For the first time in the history of the world every human being is now subjected to contact with dangerous chemicals, from the moment of conception until death.
What an appalling thought that is, Mr. Speaker.
In the less than two decades of their use, the synthetic pesticides have been so thoroughly distributed throughout the animate and inanimate world that they occur virtually everywhere. They have been recovered from most of the major river systems and even from streams of groundwater flowing unseen through the earth. Residues of these chemicals linger in soil to which they may have been applied a dozen years before. They have entered and lodged in the bodies of fish, birds, reptiles, and domestic and wild animals-
And so on. I can speak from personal experience, Mr. Speaker, of having had cattle die on the range because of eating grass 27507-3-155

The chemical weed killers are a bright new toy. They work in a spectacular way; they give a giddy sense of power over nature to those who wield them, and as for the long range and less obvious effects-these are easily brushed aside as the baseless imaginings of pessimists. About two decades later various other organic phosphates came into use as insecticides, as we have seen, and soon cases reminiscent of the ginger paralysis episode began to occur.

Mr. Speaker, in closing this debate I should like to point out that I think it is probably up to the committee itself to determine the definition of the word "marketing" in the resolution. The resolution reads in part as follows:
That a special committee be appointed to consider and report upon (a) the law and practices relating to the control of the introduction, marketing and use of drugs.
I would take it that means the control of the introduction, control of marketing and control of the use of drugs. I think the context in the resolution in which the word "marketing" is used relates to the whole process of getting drugs on the market with proper safeguards. I think it must be agreed that the problem which has brought about the proposal to establish this committee relates to drug safety and consequent implications. Let us not be sidetracked. The prime purpose of this committee is to study the quality of drugs and the consequent protection of Canadian citizens.
The report of the restrictive trade practices commission has not come down yet and when it does I believe that will be the time for the committee to decide what it might wish to do in this respect. I do implore the members of this committee not to forget the main purpose of their appointment. I would hope that the committee would get on with the objective, which involves concern for the safety of drugs.
I should like to refer to two or three things which were brought to the attention of the house by certain hon. members who have spoken. The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux) made a very considered contribution to this debate. He showed a desire to help to achieve our main objective. I should like to assure the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) the L.S.D. is available and its use will be permitted in research and clinical work. This was discussed at length when Bill No. C-3 was before the house. I know that we were quite cognizant of the desire of the house as a whole at that time and consideration has certainly been given to this matter. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), while there may have been some misunderstanding on the part of a certain institution at one stage,


this has been rectified. The drug has actually never been off the market and it has never ceased to be available for these purposes.
I should also like to assure the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that Bill No. C-3 can certainly be examined in the committee and suggestions made at that time will be given every consideration. It is perfectly all right as far as I am concerned to discuss the act in the committee.
My prime objective, Mr. Speaker, in having this committee set up is to see if there is anything further that can be done for the protection of Canadians, because in the handling of drugs we want to ensure that Canadian citizens are given every protection possible. That is the prime consideration in the formation of this committee.
The hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) inquired about the use of substances fed to or injected into poultry and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) inquired as to the effects of insecticides on wild life. Mr. Chairman, last night at ten o'clock I was seeking to make some suggestions with regard to matters which I thought the new board might consider. I was talking particularly about the fisheries of Newfoundland and Labrador and I was suggesting that one practical matter which the new board could look into was assistance for fishermen who had been away from their jobs for some time and needed to be reestablished, men who had previously been employed at other jobs and wanted to become fishermen, or those fishermen whose gear and property had become run down to a point where it was adversely affecting their incomes. I would hope that financial assistance to fishermen in these basic problems would be considered by the new board.
There are other matters I should like to touch on briefly and I will deal with them in detail when the estimates of various departments are called. There is the matter of bringing unemployment insurance for fishermen who sell their fish fresh, up to the same level as prevails in the case of those who are engaged in the salt fish business. I should like also to mention the need for community stages, adequate bait and salt supplies for the fishermen. I might mention the need for the installation along the Labrador coast of community stages which would include cookhouses and bunkhouses for summer crews. These are just some of the matters in connection with the fisheries which I would hope the new board would look into.
I referred briefly to the need for roads in Labrador and specifically to the building of roads necessary for the development of the forests of Labrador. In that connection, I should like to point out the need for federal roads to resources in the interior of Labrador. As most hon. members are aware developments are taking place in western Labrador today, the magnitude of which has seldom been seen in Canada. One of the great industrial developments of all our history is taking place, and two new towns are growing. All these matters should be examined, and particularly the matter of road building in this vast new empire should be examined.
I should like to refer specifically to Gander airport, where a great new terminal and new townsite have been established. Gander airport represents an investment of millions of dollars by the federal government. I should like the new board to look into the possibility of making use of the unused potential there. Further use of the airport could perhaps be

Atlantic Development Board. made by changing the patterns used by international air carriers. I do not know, specifically, what can be done in this respect but I do believe an attempt should be made towards the greater utilization of this airport. It might be used to a greater extent by the R.C.A.F. and this should be considered. The possibility of establishing secondary industries in the Gander area might also be considered.
In so far as the forest business in Newfoundland is concerned, may I again refer to the need for roads through these forests to aid in the protection of the forests from such pests as the woolly aphis which I mentioned last night. Thus far, I have been mentioning the spending of money but I should like it to be understood that I consider such expenditures, if recommended by the board would be in the nature of an investment rather than merely a handout to carry on under existing conditions. I do believe that the money invested in the fisheries, in the forests and in the development of our natural resources could pay rich dividends to Canada as a Whole. I should like to try to establish this principle.
With the minister's permission, I should like to mention a phrase he used in connection with the Atlantic provinces being a captive market. He hastened to add, if I remember correctly that their position on the eastern seaboard also gave them some advantages in trading. I might mention my own province, and perhaps confine my remarks to my own riding with which I happen to be most familiar. It is true that people of the Atlantic provinces provide a captive market but at the same time the products of our forests, pulp, paper and wood are exported in great quantities; our minerals are exported in large quantities, as are frozen and salted fish. These products represent many millions of dollars and practically all that money comes back to Canada. These products are not consumed in Canada, they are consumed in other countries. The money received for them is funnelled through Newfoundland-I think this applies to all the Atlantic provinces-and is largely spent in central Canada in the manufacturing areas. I make no complaint about this because this is the pattern of trade. We all benefit from trading but by and large, speaking of my own riding the millions of dollars received for the products exported are returned to Canada through Newfoundland.
The point I wish to make is that, that being so, when we ask for assistance to develop our particular part of Canada we are really asking for some of our own back. We would like to get it back in a way which would enable us to earn more to improve and to increase our industrial capacity, so that not only will

we benefit but Canada as a whole will benefit from this investment in the Atlantic provinces, the oldest and still one of the greatest parts of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity to enter this debate on a measure which is vitally important to all of those who come from those provinces by the sea and to add to the contribution which has been made by so many hon. members from the Atlantic provinces. I feel it is especially fitting that this resolution to establish an Atlantic development board should be in the name of the Minister of National Revenue, New Brunswick's representative in the government of Canada. As we all know, for eight years during which our province of New Brunswick forged steadily ahead, the minister was the premier of New Brunswick. He is now an able and persistent advocate for the maritimes in the government of Canada.
There is no question, Mr. Chairman, that for the past century maritime development has lagged behind the rest of Canada. Perhaps it is unfortunate we did not unite before confederation into one province and we would then have entered as one unit speaking with one strong voice, instead of the four which have so many times seemed to be speaking at cross purposes. Since we cannot change history, we must make the best of it. I believe that there have been certain beneficial effects of confederation and these can be seen when we look at the condition of our three maritime provinces of Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia as compared with the position of Newfoundland before 1949.
It seems to me that one of our troubles in the maritimes is that for so long we have stressed maritime weaknesses instead of stressing maritime possibilities. Certainly, we have weaknesses. We have had over the years the problem of the three terrible T's, as we call them, transportation, tariffs and taxes. But we have always had, and we will have, the lumber, fish and minerals and more important, we have the people, the greatest resource of all. In order to evaluate the ability of maritimers we need only look at the leaders in the professions, in industry, in banking and commerce, both in Canada and abroad. In every one of these, maritimers occupy prominent and often front rank positions. What we seem to lack is the necessary enterprise, the spirit of co-operation, the willingness to experiment. Not only have we lacked cooperation between the different provinces but even between different groups in the same province. And, of course, for far too many

years there was little or no co-operation between the provincial and federal governments. This situation has been greatly improved in the last five years.
This resolution calls for the establishment of an Atlantic development board. This is something we promised in the last election campaign. Personally, Mr. Chairman, I am very proud, as I am sure other Conservatives are, to be a member of this house on this occasion as we see this first step being taken to fulfil that promise. In that connection, the composition of the board will be a very pertinent factor, one of the most important factors of all. I would urge upon the government the necessity for searching out the very best men that are available for appointment to this board.
I suggest to the government, and I suggest this as a Conservative member, that we should not just appoint men for political reasons, but let us have skilled men, engineers, economists and industrialists, men like Mr. Michael Wardell and men like Professor William Smith, former president of APEC and now head of the department of economics in the University of New Brunswick.
One might ask what there is to develop. Well there are a great many things and we have heard about them many times in this house. I suppose some hon. members would like us to stop talking about them, but there are so many things we want developed in the maritime provinces, projects such as the causeway, the Corridor road, the Chignecto canal both for transportation as a power complex and the Passamaquoddy power project. We also want further development on the Saint John river for hydro purposes and further development of industries at all levels.
In the past five years we have seen the erection of many public buildings in many of our constituencies in the east, including my own. I would like to agree with the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo when he discussed the principle of small industries in our Atlantic provinces. I would much rather see constructed one manufacturing plant in my constituency that would hire 500 men all the year round than all the public buildings that have been built in York-Sunbury since confederation.
One example of this possibility is the railway town of McAdam, which has been vitally affected by dieselization. It is on the Canadian Pacific main line and perhaps too many members do not know McAdam, as most passengers pass through there at six o'clock in the morning travelling east on the Canadian Pacific. For many years it had a very vital transportation industry, but because of dieselization the town has gone down. It is a town which has ample electric power and
Atlantic Development Board a good water supply, and it also has an excellent labour force. Today it has the necessary buildings available for new industry. What better site could we find for a new industry?
I suggest that the board, when it is established, should do its best to seek out small industries and bring them into towns such as McAdam. I would much rather see a portion of the hundreds of millions of dollars now being spent on unemployment insurance and welfare services being put into the creation of new industries and re-vitalizing of existing ones.
It is true that some measure of social assistance is necessary. There are always people who, through no fault of their own, need our help, but I am concerned with the fact that in this welfare state, into which we have drifted during the last 30 or 35 years, wherein everyone takes in everyone else's washing, that there are far too many people today who would rather collect unemployment insurance than do their share of the washing. Living off social welfare has become a way of life for some Canadians, even unto the second and third generations.
It is too bad that so many politicians do not have the moral courage to face this problem and take the necessary action. I know that in my constituency, as in all the Atlantic provinces, there are many fine citizens who would much rather work than draw unemployment insurance.
For the past ten years businessmen, economists and professional men in the maritimes have been attempting to lift themselves up by the bootstraps through the Atlantic provinces economic council, which is an independent, non-political organization formed some eight years ago with the aim of accelerating the economic development of the Atlantic provinces. APEC has often been mentioned in this house and I feel it has done a magnificent job. We all wish it well in the future.
Two years ago the premiers of the four Atlantic provinces concerned about the problem with which this bill deals today, brought Professor A. K. Cairncross from Great Britain to conduct a thorough survey of the Atlantic economy. I might add that today he is economic advisor to the government of Great Britain. He was invited over by premiers Stanfield, Flemming, Shaw and Premier Smallwood of Newfoundland. In his investigation he brought forward a number of conclusions which I would like to put on the record. He said in effect that (1) in various respects the Atlantic provinces are lagging behind the rest of Canada. The most important form taken by this lag is the absence of

Atlantic Development Board opportunities of employment particularly employment that is regular, full-time, and in well paid occupations. He said (2) the main cause of this lag lies in the rapid decline in employment in the resource-based industries of the region; then (3) this decline, which seems unlikely to be reversed, will give rise to a growing surplus of labour in view of the high natural increase of population in the region, unless migration takes place on a larger scale or new industries are established.
We do not want our people to go away; we want industries established where our people are. Professor Cairncross also said it would be desirable to review the implications of doubling manufacturing employment, that is, employment in non-primary industries, over the next 20 years, in order to establish what contribution this might make to total employment in the area and whether expansion on this scale would be practicable, viewed in relation to the simultaneous growth of new industry in Canada, and what incentives could usefully be offered in order to attract industry to the area.
Point No. 5 was that a review in similar terms might be undertaken for the island of Newfoundland, including Labrador. I am sure the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador would agree to the inclusion of Labrador in this connection.
Professor Cairncross further said that although there are a number of handicaps, arising chiefly from distance from markets, facing manufacturers in the Atlantic provinces, these handicaps would not be fatal to a number of industries in which transport costs are relatively low provided (a) these industries were assured of some initial help towards the cost of establishing new productive units and (b) that they could count on some further assistance for a longer period.
He also said that the most powerful immediate attractions to businesses contemplating production in the Atlantic provinces are likely to be modern factories ready for occupation, offered at less than an economic rent for a limited period of years; and a grant towards the cost of training labour, bringing in skilled workers, moving plant and machinery, and other settling-in expenses.
Then he says there are also many noneconomic factors of almost equal importance in the framing of an initial decision by management-the amenities of the area, its educational facilities, the reputation of its workers, and the sense of purposefulness and aliveness that it is able to communicate. New businesses, especially those coming from elsewhere, will also want to satisfy themselves that their long term prospects in an Atlantic location compare favourably with their
[Mr. MacRae.l

prospects elsewhere. They would be likely to have some advantage in labour costs but this would usually appear insufficient to offset the disadvantage of comparative remoteness from markets.
Therefore they would be likely to require further inducements outlasting the settling-in period, and these could include any of the following: (a) a subsidy to freight costs, especially outward freights; (b) various forms of tax incentive; (c) capital grants or guarantees and (d) a government undertaking to provide a market for part or all of the output of the business.
I may add that the last two are highly effective but are not always practical, and sometimes politics enter into them. The first introduces no new point of principle. It is a logical way of reducing the inconvenience of distance and was fully investigated by the MacPherson commission on transportation.
Point No. 12 is that tax incentives have been used by a number of countries with varying success. In some they have attracted industries from other countries, while in others where the main object was to attract businesses to one region from the rest of a country, their usefulness appears to have been limited. If tax incentives are used in Canada it would be best for the provincial governments to conclude a tax treaty with each applicant satisfying the statutory conditions, and then make reimbursement annually of whatever taxes were agreed upon in the treaty.
The fourteenth point is that it would also be desirable that the federal government should regulate the use of such incentives, if adopted, reimbursing provincial governments for their outlays, provided they complied with the common regulations governing tax concessions. Then he says that whatever is done to attract new industry to the region would be slow in taking effect and should not be postponed or abandoned because of any temporary slowing down of development elsewhere in Canada. I repeat that it should not be postponed or abandoned because of any temporary slowing down of development elsewhere in Canada.
He adds that nothing that is done to promote industrial development in the Atlantic provinces should override the prior need to increase the efficiency and expand the markets of the primary industries of the region. I said this before, Mr. Chairman, that there must be no second-class citizens in Canada, and there must be no second-class areas in Canada. Those of us who come from the Atlantic provinces will never be content to accept such things.
Before I sit down I would like personally to congratulate the hon. members from the

Atlantic provinces who are supporting this measure today and I would ask them to continue to give the minister their full and unqualified support. Finally, in closing, I have mentioned that we should find the very best men we can for this Atlantic development board. That idea is exemplified in the following words in the foreword to "Creative Canadian Capital" published by Canadian Enterprise Development Corporation Limited.
I would like to close with these words:
Seek out creative men with the vision of things to be done. Help breathe life into new ideas and processes and products with money-and with more than money-with sensitive appreciation for creative drive; with support in management and manpower, with loyalty to the idea and to its initiator, the creative man.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will not take up too much time but I just want to say a few words on this bill because it affects the Atlantic provinces. First of all I should like to say that the minister who introduced this bill is certainly one of our most outstanding citizens in New Brunswick and has made a great contribution to that province. Nevertheless I do not think he is the proper man to introduce this bill and I regret that the Minister of Finance has not seen fit to take a more active part in this matter, because our problem is not revenue, it is the lack of revenue. We have a very high regard for him. He is the fourth minister of finance since confederation, I believe, to come from the Atlantic provinces.

In the Canadian National Railways shops at Moncton over 300 men have been laid off during the past five years. The passenger shop in Moncton has been transferred to Winnipeg. The men employed in the Moncton shop were told to go to Winnipeg or be without a job. That is the type of assistance we have been getting for the Atlantic provinces, and it has created

I think the hon. member for York-Sunbury was very realistic in his views, but yesterday when we listened to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg we must have all felt that when we die we do not want to go to heaven but to the maritime provinces because he really painted a wonderful picture. However, I might say that I have a very high regard for his country because my wife happens to come from there.
Mr. Chairman, I want to deal with the question of tax rental agreements for a moment; that is, what we receive in the province of New Brunswick and what it has amounted to in the past. I am talking about the good faith which the government assume they have shown. The amount we received was reduced because, I assume, our showing has not been very good in past elections. The result was that we suffered. I know that in my own city of Moncton we were cut back to the amount of $62,000, which amounted to eight cents on our municipal tax rates. This is the sort of concession we have been getting from the provincial government in view of the decisions of the federal government. The bill is probably a step in the right direction, but it does not contain those things in which we are interested in the maritimes.
I was quite amused not too long ago when going through Port Elgin to see a sign on a government wharf saying, "People using this wharf do so at their own risk". I think it was Lincoln who said 100 years ago that you cannot be for and against the same thing at the same time. Yet the government now tells us that we are going to be in a semiutopia with this new board. We are told there are going to be all kinds of public works, and at the same time they have cut their program in the Atlantic provinces by many millions of dollars, due to the austerity program. Wharves, all kinds of public buildings and all kinds of employment have been affected because of the austerity program. That is another reason, Mr. Chairman, why I wish the Minister of Finance had taken a part in this debate.
The Atlantic provinces are certainly in need of a gigantic public works program. I have discussed this question with the Minister of Transport with the idea of getting our runways in Moncton lengthened so that we can take on the larger aircraft. I might say that in terms of arrivals and departures we are the eighth largest airport in Canada. However, this has not been done; the program has been cut. All these various avenues which the government could have pursued in order to bring about more employment and better conditions have been ignored. Therefore I say that the government has not

Although the maritimer is a dedicated person generally, I cannot see too many of them working on a part time basis for $3,000 a year, however much I would like to see this type of man on the board. Again I point out that the government has cut its own public works program. The other day I called to the attention of the house the situation at Scoudouc where men had been laid off in the R.C.A.F. If the government really meant well it would not be cutting down on its own estimates and those of its agencies in the Atlantic provinces. I think the same thing applies to the railway where there have been tremendous cuts. This, too, is an agency of government. I suggest that the government, in setting up this board, should review the situation to which I have drawn attention, bearing in mind such cases as the No. 5 equipment depot in Moncton where the fire department has been abolished. These people came to the city and were looking for employment, and some were hired.
Again let me say I am sorry the Minister of Fisheries could not find time to take part in this debate. I say this because the fishing industry is one of our most important industries. I must say I am critical of those two ministers I have mentioned because this is a matter of such importance to us that they should have been here to take part in the debate. I say this of the Minister of Finance because, certainly, what we need in the Atlantic provinces is money.
I do not intend to prolong this. I want it understood that I shall be pleased to go along with the bill though, frankly, I cannot see too much in it. I hope the minister when he replies will endeavour to explain more precisely to us what this is going to mean -how we are going to be rewarded if we go along with this proposal. Then, again, I am concerned as to whether there is likely to be a conflict between the board whose formation we are now considering and the national board, although I must admit I am not familiar with just what powers the national board is to have. In any case it would appear that one must be subservient to the other.
In closing, if this board is to be the answer to the ills of the maritimes I urge those ministers concerned to take a closer look at the public works program which was cancelled in the Atlantic provinces within the last three or four months, and to examine the cuts made by the various government agencies in the provinces, such as the C.N.R. It is common knowledge that their operating budget was cut by over $3 million in the Atlantic provinces for the coming year. I repeat, you cannot be both for and against the same thing at the same time.

Mr. Chairman, I regret not to say, as several others have said, that I do not have a long speech to deliver before the adoption of this measure. Without being an expert linguist, I wonder whether it would not be a good thing to point out that this word "office" is not the proper term for the French translation of the title of this bill. In fact, if we consider that the word "office" means much more a function or a group of functions than a body-although I know there are several expert linguists in the Department of National Revenue, as well as in the other divisions of the government-I submit it would perhaps be a good thing to substitute for the word "office" the word "conseil".
Now, if we refer to various dictionaries, and among the most important, we note that this word means much more a series of functions than a body. Now, I would not dare believe that the government would like this body to play the role described by the word "office" in Quillet, a well-known dictionary which gives the following definition of the word "office", used in an administrative sense:

Atlantic Development Board The setting up of "offices" is to let certain industrial and commercial establishments escape from the rules of public accounting and to bring them as close as possible to private management procedures.
I do not think it is the aim of the government to have this body escape from the control of the government.
That is my suggestion, and after having consulted its expert linguists, the government may, if it is advisable, propose the appropriate amendment. If it does, I will have contributed a little to a better interpretation of this legislation and especially to its being more adequately titled.
