Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has sponsored my former leader and present colleague for the ministry of public works. May I say to him that I would be only too glad to second the nomination because I think that anyone who lived and worked in New Brunswick between the years 1952 and 1960 will quite understand the qualifications of the Minister of National Revenue for the ministry of public works, and New Brunswick and Canada, in fact, would be well served if it were to occur. This is about as relevant, as the electioneering tactic involving the Prince Edward Island causeway, which has been introduced into this debate by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Obviously a bold, imaginative and extremely expensive project of this sort needs engineering studies. I do not think these engineering studies are inconsistent with economic studies. Obviously when a project like this will link the island with the mainland of Canada there will be features which will have to be studied by the Atlantic development board. New industries will be started in Prince Edward Island and, in fact, there will be an entirely new economic outlook, and I would certainly hope that aspect would be considered by the board when it is set up.
I have listened to the debate in the past few days and I had hoped that it would progress a little more speedily than it has but it does not appear that that is going to be the case. I had also hoped that more members from other parts of the country would participate in the debate. The leader of the New Democratic party and a member from one of the Toronto ridings did participate, and in my opinion this is useful.
The proposal now before us is another phase of a long term attack on the material problems facing the Atlantic provinces, but the attack must be as well an attack on people's attitudes. I think most of those who represent constituencies in eastern Canada understand what I mean. In my view people's

attitudes and people's approaches have to be discussed here. I noted a phrase in a book I read recently by Joseph Kraft entitled "The Grand Design". In it he was talking about the problems facing the underdeveloped countries of the world. He said that what these countries lack seemed to him to be somewhat of a litany of the damned. Sometimes the people of the Atlantic provinces tend to talk of their disabilities in somewhat the same manner. I hope there is not a litany of the damned in the Atlantic provinces and I am optimistic enough to think that this board, in co-operation with the national economic development board, the productivity council, governments, APEC and people of good will, can help to solve our economic problems.
I was very interested in the speech of the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough when he recalled again-I think it cannot be recalled too often-the three main problems facing those of us who live in the Atlantic provinces. I think it is well for members of all parties to recall the problems of transportation, the problems of lack of capital development and so on.
I do not see any magic formulae in this board. We live in an age when people expect members of parliament and governments to wave wands and bring about revolutionary solutions to problems. There is no panacea within the words of this legislation that can bring an end to all the problems facing us. Our economic problems will not suddenly disappear because this board is set up. The hon. member for Gloucester referred to the plans of the former Liberal government with respect to a power grid. I think they were reasonable plans but not as good as the plans of the present government, because the grid was to be operated by a federal government power company, the Northern Power Company, as I remember, whereas we have a very capable electric power commission in New Brunswick which is doing a much more intimate job, shall we say, on the site rather than the direction coming from Ottawa. The power grid is working out and I think it is a forerunner of the national power grid referred to in the speech from the throne. I hope that any power grid will take into account the need for the use of coal for thermal power production. In my view this is the helpful thing about the grid. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned Hamilton falls. I agree that it must be developed, but I think it must be developed in tune with the coal aspect of power production.
I feel, too, that the recommendations of the royal commission on transportation will

be helpful to the transportation problem facing the maritimes when they are implemented in statute form. I prefer government policies which will bring a return in human living conditions for the money spent. I think there is too much of this business of handing out large cheques or saying a solution of a problem can be arrived at by merely paying another grant or another subsidy. Subsidies and grants are part of the formula for a solution of our problem. I think some of the solutions have been based too much on the money aspect.
I am optimistic enough to believe that this board will be unorthodox in its acceptance of new proposals which will improve all the resources of this part of Canada, and that Canada will not just be enriched by the migration of people from the Atlantic provinces. I hope that the area itself will be built up to assist the people in that area. I had, too, a thought about the very name of this bill. We have had a sort of evolution of feeling in the Atlantic provinces. I am not going to say who started it or when it started. These jousting matches are so unrealistic that they are not listened to by the people of Canada. I do suggest this, that the founding of the Atlantic provinces economic council in 1952 was a highwater mark. I think the meeting of the premiers-I do not care who the premiers were, although I am proud that the sponsor of this bill was one of the important keystones of that meeting-was an important step. The very fact that APEC started and that the Atlantic premiers got together resulted in the fact that today we have a bill presented to this house containing the words "Atlantic provinces board". It is not the Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, New Brunswick or Nova Scotia board. I suggest this denotes a change in thinking. It shows that the maritimes and Newfoundland are growing up and, I believe it shows we have come a long way.
Now, a great deal has been made about the capital projects aspect. Perhaps I am naive about these things, but surely the board will study these capital projects and make recommendations to parliament. Then, parliament will vote the money. At least, I presume that is the way the board will operate. In so far as the problem referred to by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough is concerned, the meetings of the board, I think he will find if he consults his legal colleagues that this is the usual device to provide the widest possible scope for meetings. The only provision tying down the meetings is that one meeting a year will be held here in Ottawa. Otherwise, the board can meet twice a week or even daily in accordance with the provisions of that section.
Atlantic Development Board
I have only one other suggestion, Mr. Chairman. During the course of this debate someone mentioned the migration from the maritimes. I think this is true. I like to add to that the fact that because of this migration we in the Atlantic part of Canada have not had the benefit of a transfusion of immigrants. A good many people have left the Atlantic provinces for other parts of Canada and of the world, but we have not shared in that transfusion that has made, if I may be so bold as to say it, Toronto an interesting city and made other parts of Canada much more cosmopolitan than would otherwise have been the case. I feel optimistic about this board because I think this is part of the pattern of the recognition of the special problems of Atlantic Canada by the rest of the country. Obviously, the former government made contributions to this change in attitude. Obviously, too, the present government has set an example of assistance to Atlantic Canada which bodes well for the helpfulness of this board we are considering today.

I would also bring to the attention of the minister a short visit which was made to Ottawa last spring by the premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. They presented the Prime Minister with a brief, which had been prepared after considerable study by the power authorities and research boards of the two provinces, but even two or three months after that the ministers of the departments concerned did not know about it. The brief was shelved and put away, and I question whether this board would have more effect on the government than the recommendations made by Premier Stanfield of Nova Scotia and Premier Robichaud of New Brunswick.

Atlantic Development Board all those things which go to the determination of whether or not there should be established in the Atlantic provinces an industry based on certain assumptions of raw material and available markets. That is my own feeling about what they might do.

There are many businesses which are not able to take part in research to any great extent, possibly for financial reasons. The hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador also said that this should be a matter of investment rather than handouts. I could not agree more with that observation. I said the other day that I felt the Atlantic economic development board had great possibilities. I repeat that. This is the most forward step which has been taken in my lifetime by the federal authority. This is a recognition of the special circumstances existing in the Atlantic provinces. I hope all of us will be prepared to pass the bill. If we were to find some weaknesses in it in the course of

Atlantic Development Board its operation in the coming year, then we could come back and ask for amendments to strengthen it. At this time I feel it is in the nature of an experiment. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-25, to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill is the same as the one which was introduced last session and which was debated on March 23 last. I do not intend to repeat the argument I made on that occasion as the debate of last session is recorded at page 2145 of Hansard and is available to all hon. members. However, I should like to take a few minutes in order to reply briefly to some of the arguments made by hon. members who took part in this debate and also to clear up what appears to be some misunderstanding about the bill.
When I introduced this bill last session I referred to it as a very simple one as, in fact, it really is. Some hon. members took issue with that statement. However, I should like to refer in particular to the observations made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris) who at that time was parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I single out this argument as it is typical of all the arguments that were made in that debate and it illustrates the misunderstanding on which those arguments were based. I am reading from page 2146 of Hansard of March 23, 1962, beginning at the second column. The then parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce is speaking and this is what he said:
Mr. Speaker, what would the amendment before us seek to do? The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) would seek to amend section 30(2) of the present legislation in order to empower the merchant seamen compensation board to name as foster mother someone who would take care of a child or children of a deceased seaman in another home, not the existing household of the deceased seaman or of the deceased seaman's family. This amendment would have the effect of entitling the foster mother to the widow's pension of $75 a month as long as she was caring for the children up to the age of 18 years, or in the case of an invalid child, beyond that age. That would be the situation if the seaman died leaving no widow.
That quotation contains the main argument that was brought forward against adopting this legislation. It was contended that the purpose of the original bill was to keep the family together and that the amendment which I was introducing then, and am introducing again today, would break the family up or divide the family and therefore prevent the main object of the legislation from being implemented.
In this connection I wish to point out first and foremost that this bill does nothing of the kind. It does not compel the merchant seamen compensation board to do anything it is not compelled to do under the present legislation. All it does is to give the compensation board more discretion so that they can deal with various types of cases. We all realize that when a number of children are orphaned, it is desirable to keep the family
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act together as much as possible. However, there are cases in which there is only one child. There are cases in which the family cannot be kept together. In those cases some other provision must be made for them. However, under the present legislation that provision cannot be made. If provisions are made which are in the best interests of the child, then the person or the foster parent is penalized as a result. That brings me to the second purpose of this bill which is really to enable the merchant seamen compensation board to make better provision for the welfare of the orphaned children or the orphaned child and to be able to do it without penalizing the person who undertakes this responsibility.
In the quotation I just read from Hansard there is just one point I wish to repeat:
This amendment would have the effect of entitling the foster mother to the widow's pension of $75 a month as long as she was caring for the children up to the age of 18 years-
What the parliamentary secretary did not say-and this is the great omission in this case-is that for that mother or foster mother to get the full pension of $75 a month under the present act, that foster mother must move into the home which belongs to the deceased parent. In this connection, I wish to ask two questions. Who can expect to get a foster mother-or anybody else for that matter- to move into a home, undertake the care and the maintenance of the home, the care of the children, supply them with food and clothing and keep up a shelter for $75 a month? Certainly the day is gone when it is realistic to expect a person to be able to do that. I think that emphasizes the need for some change in this particular law. The real trouble is that the present law is not flexible enough to deal with the many different types of cases that must be dealt with. I know of some in my riding. That is why I am particularly interested in this bill.
During the election campaign last June I made a particular point of visiting one of these orphans. This was a single child and it was impossible to get anybody to move into the house which had belonged to the child's parents. As I said before, the remuneration of $75 a month is not enough to induce anybody to take that responsibility. So the only alternative was to move the child to somebody else's house. In this case that is the only thing that could be done; but because that was done, because the person looking after the child did not move with her children into the house of the orphan's deceased parents she could not get the full allowance. Do you know how much she has been getting on
2460	HOUSE OF
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act behalf of that child simply because it was impossible for her to move into the house occupied by the parents of the deceased? Instead of the $75 she could have got which, as I said, would have been inadequate, she could only get $20 a month because the child was moved into her house, which was a much better and more comfortable home than the child had ever had before. That is all that has been paid for that child throughout the years.
The child is now 14 or 15 years of age and there are school expenses, which means that $20 is not adequate. If this amendment were made the merchant seamen's compensation board in any case would have discretion to make the arrangements that have to be made and would be able to remunerate the person suitably and more equitably than is the case at the present time.
I do not want to take too much time because other members want to speak on this bill, but I wish to emphasize again that the bill does not compel the board to separate families. The board still has the discretion it has always had and if they feel that the best thing to do is to keep the family together under one roof, then the bill does not stop them from doing so. They could do so before and they can do so under this bill. In this day and age it is very unlikely you will get anyone to accept such a responsibility for $75 a month. The bill does not interfere with the board's judgment in any way. It is a very simple bill designed merely to give the board more freedom to act, more freedom to deal with different types of cases and to deal with them in a better way. Therefore I hope that the bill will receive the support of the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. Baldwin (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PAYMENTS FOR ORPHANS OF SEAMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that a landlubber from the inland port of Peace River may be permitted to participate in the debate on this bill in respect to which I commend the hon. member for the humanitarian motives which appear to actuate him in bringing this matter to the attention of the house. I am not raising any formal objection


but I should like to call the hon. member's attention to something to which he might well give some consideration before this matter reaches the stage when it is voted on, and I may say that what I have in mind is accentuated by the answer made by the hon. member to the question asked by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works.
I would point out that this is a bill which in its result may well have the effect of extending the terms of payment of a fund to a larger number of people than have been permitted to participate in its benefits up to now. Whether it is considered to be a fund which the crown is directly or indirectly distributing, or whether it is more on the basis of an insurance fund, as in the case of most compensation boards, may be an issue; but if it is in fact considered a fund which the crown is distributing then the hon. member is seeking as a private member, even with the most laudable objectives, to extend the number of people who may recover from the fund. I simply bring this matter to his attention. I am not raising it as a formal point of order but mentioning it now for consideration later.
I am inclined to the view that the hon. member may well have misconceived or misinterpreted the legislation. The act which he wishes to deal with, of course, is the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act and the particular section he is dealing with is section 30, subsection 2, which reads in part as follows:
Where the seaman leaves no widow or the widow subsequently dies, and it seems desirable to continue the existing household-
I think he has given to the word "household" an interpretation which substantially strains the meaning. I think he connotes household with house, and I do not think this is the intention at all. As I read the act, and I went through it briefly today, this particular subsection is an attempt to retain intact the domestic family which survives the death of (a) the seaman or (b) the widow of the seaman. I do not think it matters at all where the household, and by that I mean the family, is maintained. Whether it be in the house where the seaman or widow died or whether it be in the house of the proposed foster parents, as long as the household or family is maintained intact as a unit under the normal provisions with regard to a family, then there is eligibility for the foster mother to receive this additional payment.
I have a dictionary here, a reasonably compact one which I can master in the house- Thorndike-Barnhart-and I refer to the meaning of the word "household" given in that dictionary:
All the people living in a house; family; family and servants; a royal household.

And so on. I think that section 30 is quite plain and specific. It simply says that a person qualifies to receive this additional benefit provided the household, meaning the family, is retained intact. In the explanatory notes to the bill the hon. member also labours under this misapprehension because he says there:
Under the present wording, the allowance is paid only if the person moves into the household of the deceased seaman or deceased seaman's widow.
Now, if you delete the word "household" and substitute for it the word "house", then I think my hon. friend would be correct. I suggest that in his amendment he has attempted to use the words "domestic establishment" and I imagine he has used those words in an attempt to distinguish between the word "household" and the sort of thing he has in mind. In looking at the same dictionary, I find that the word "establishment" has a number of meanings one of which is household. I think, and I submit this with some strength, that although I do not know what interpretation may have been placed upon this by the board-I am going to come to that in a minute-I would say that the act as it is now achieves the result which the hon. gentleman feels can only be achieved by his amendment.
I should like to refer to section 14 of the act itself. This is the type of section we see in all these compensation acts. I quote:
The board has exclusive jurisdiction to examine into, hear and determine all matters and questions arising under this act and as to any matter or thing in respect of which any power, authority or discretion is conferred upon the board, and the action or decision of the board thereon is final and conclusive and is not open to question or review in any court-
This section has been the subject of a considerable number of judicial interpretations. As a matter of fact, I had the misfortune to run up against one of them myself. I think this question has even been taken to the Supreme Court of Canada, and it has been ruled this sort of section in a compensation act means exactly what it says. This is something we cannot say about all legislation. The boards constituted under compensation legislation have absolutely no impediment in interpreting an act. For example, they can decide who is eligible, decide the extent of injuries and who is entitled to the payment of benefits under the act.
My suggestion is that instead of bringing this forward as an issue to be debated in parliament, the proper authority to whom these representations should be made is the board. It may well be that I am labouring under a misapprehension. It may well be that a decision has been made by the board on this matter. I would say to the hon. member
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act that if he can be as eloquent in taking his case before the board as he has been before this house, there is no reason why he cannot persuade the board, which is not bound by precedent and is able to amend or vary its decisions, to accept the validity of his argument and make the corresponding changes.
I mention that because I see this act was originally passed in 1946, was introduced into the revised statutes in 1952 as chapter 178, and has since been amended in 1952-53 and in 1957. I just had a moment to look through the 1957 debates. I observed that this particular section, not the subsection but section 30, was the subject of an amendment and of a considerable amount of discussion. At that time, of course, conditions were reversed and hon. members who are now in opposition were sitting on this side of the house. The hon. member who sponsored this bill spoke in connection with this particular amendment in 1957. I could be unkind, possibly, and suggest that certain legislation which in 1957, in the opinion of hon. members opposite, was scintillating, bright and needed no amendment, suddenly after 1957, upon mature reflection and consideration, appeared to be not quite as suitable. This may well be the case, but I am not suggesting it is.
In 1957, the hon. member made no reference to this particular aspect of the act. It may well be that from then until he introduced his bill cases may have been brought to his attention which did not exist before. If so, of course, that would be a good reason for introducing this measure at this time. I feel that when we attempt to vary, mould or amend laws to meet every case, even a few isolated cases, we frequently get ourselves into difficulty. Where you have an act which gives a board that broad jurisdiction which is given under section 14, it seems to me that board is the place where representations should be made. Possibly the hon. gentleman may have an opportunity of telling me later that the board has made firm decisions on this point. I feel that with a logical and reasonable interpretation of the section as it now stands, and with the cooperation of the board, everything which he asks in this bill can now be obtained. Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief remarks on Bill C-25 now under discussion and entitled, an Act to amend the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act.
This bill provides a wider choice of residence for the persons who accept to care for children who have been prematurely deprived of their parents.
2462	HOUSE OF
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act
Under paragraph (2) of section 30 of the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act, it seems that a sister, an aunt or any other person called upon to care for the children of deceased seamen, is obliged to move into the former household. In my opinion, such a restriction should be abolished, and I feel that the mover of this bill has taken a right view of things, since he represents a maritime district and he may be better aware than many of us of the problems resulting from the provisions of the act, especially in paragraph (2) of section 30.
Mr. Speaker, not only am I not a seaman, but I do not represent a region where seamen live. The riding I have the honour of representing is located in the hinterland, but nevertheless I want to support the efforts of the mover of this bill and I also want to assure him of the support of the people in my riding.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the proposed amendment to the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act will be adopted, because it will take a great load off our seamen's minds.
I support the bill because the Social Credit party, of which I am a member, is the defender of freedom and is in favour of everything that is conducive to that freedom. In fact, the Social Crediters have proved it many times since the beginning of the session and will certainly keep on proving it.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian merchant seamen have rendered great services to their country and since they have to work in extremely dangerous conditions at times, we should see to it that in case of sudden death, their families would be secure and could move somewhere else if they wish to do so.
I can understand that after the death of the head of the family, a widow or the person who is entrusted with the care of the children may want to change domicile. Those people should be free to choose where they want to live without any risk of losing the compensation under the act.
Thanks to this legislation, it may be easier to find kindhearted individuals to look after the education of those unfortunate children. In fact, as the mover of the bill stated, the law is so restrictive at present that it may easily scare anyone who might be willing to take on such a responsibility. That is why I am in favour of the bill and I hope that it will go through so that people will be encouraged to take care of those orphans.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of this party are once


again quite pleased to support the principle of this bill and I, as a member coming from British Columbia, which is a maritime province, am very pleased to support it because there must be similar circumstances on the Pacific coast to those on the Atlantic.
The purpose of the bill is to meet circumstances which time and experience in the administration of the act have proven cannot be met without amendment to the act. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has a certain necessary function to perform with respect to a bill like this. I am not blaming him as an individual, but I thought he was using rather legalistic arguments. I could see he was experiencing heavy weather in giving a narrow legal argument in opposition to the principle of the bill; but hon. members in all parties who supported legislation in years gone past and thought the legislation was quite satisfactory have later, in the light of experience, found themselves proposing amendments to it. That is exactly the situation with respect to this bill.
The hon. member for Peace River, or to give him his due status in society, the parliamentary secretary, mentioned something to the effect that the hon. member who introduced the bill failed to introduce this amendment prior to 1957; but no doubt in the meantime the hon. member has gained much experience and knowledge as a result of representations made to him by the seamen or relatives of the seamen and saw the necessity for this amendment.
The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) and I have sharply differed on a number of occasions in this house, but on this occasion I give the hon. member full credit for having a close personal knowledge of the circumstances that warrant this amendment to the act, the circumstances under which seamen are employed, and the circumstances surrounding the administration of the act. During the years in which he has been a member of the veterans affairs committee he has demonstrated that he has a very sound knowledge of sea-going affairs, because of the riding which he represents and the circumstances under which he lives.
So far as this group are concerned, we are convinced he has advanced sound arguments in support of the amendment to show that it will be fair to the employers and will be of no expense to the consolidated revenue fund. If the parliamentary secretary has any doubt as to the cost of this amendment to the employers, I suggest he would be well advised to support the bill and then move that it be sent to the industrial

relations committee where it could be studied and witnesses called representing the seamen, the employers and any other groups who have personal knowledge of the circumstances which have prompted the hon. member to introduce the bill.
I cannot accept the narrow, legalistic argument of the parliamentary secretary, and his suggestion that the place for the hon. member to make his representations is before the board. The experience of hon. members of the house in making representations before boards has proven that to be a rather fruitless procedure. We have even had the premiers of provinces recently making representations to the board of transport commissioners with respect to the discontinuance of train and passenger services.
I suggest hon. members would be very well advised to ignore the suggestion of the parliamentary secretary and support the bill, so that the people it is intended to serve will benefit as quickly as possible.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PAYMENTS FOR ORPHANS OF SEAMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to register my support for the amendment to the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act proposed by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. I do so for one particular reason and that is that I believe the amendment is necessary. I agree that sometimes laws are made and it is not necessary to amend them; but all hon. members in the house know that certain laws, in the light of experience, have to be amended, and this is just one case where an amendment is really necessary.
The important thing to bear in mind is the welfare of the child or children involved. It may be possible in some cases to find a woman to take care of one or more children in the home where the children were born, but it is not always possible to do that. Sometimes a man or woman can be found who will look after children in his or her own home but who would not move to the original home of the children. In such a case, and if the children are going to be better cared for in the home of the foster parent, then the board should have the right to say that the maximum compensation will be paid to the person looking after the children.
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act
This amendment would give the board wider latitude in looking after such cases, and these cases really need attention.
Quite often when an explanation is demanded from the board, the reason which the board gives for not making the maximum allowance to a child is that the child is not living in its original home, and one can assume that if the child were living in its original home it would receive the maximum benefit permissible under the act.
The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Mc-Cleave) wanted to know the number of children involved. I recognize that legislation should not be made to cater to individual cases; but if legislation can be amended to make it more applicable to individual cases, I think that should be done. I do not think the number of children involved is an important question here. I was very interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Peace Paver and I must admit that his interpretation of the word "household" corresponds with mine. I believe that if the board were entitled to use that interpretation of the word "household" the full purpose of this amendment would be achieved. If "household" were to mean the home in which the child was born or the home in which the foster parent lived then the purpose of the amendment proposed by the hon. member would be achieved perfectly.
The hon. member for Peace River also made reference to the amount of money that might have to be spent in an increasing quantity if more of these cases were allowed under this act. I should point out to him that at the bottom of the explanatory notes this statement is made:
The costs of the administration of the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act and the compensation payable thereunder are chargeable to the employers and not against the consolidated revenue fund.
I think there are cases where, because this section of the act is not interpreted generously enough, some children of merchant seamen are not receiving the allowance which they should receive. I think a change needs to be made in the legislation so that the board will be given the latitude which will allow them to decide that a child or children, if they are going to be more properly cared for in the home of the foster parent, may live in the home of the foster parent and receive the maximum allowance which they would receive if they were living in the original home.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. J. McCleave (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING PAYMENTS FOR ORPHANS OF SEAMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not quarrel with the laudability of the amendment presented to us this afternoon or the most interesting speech by the
2484	HOUSE OF
Merchant Seamen Compensation Act hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter). However, I should like to point out what I regard as the main principle of his bill and one to which the house should give consideration. I would ask the question whether in cases of this kind we should proceed on the basis of legislation comparable to workmen's compensation plans in the provinces or on the basis of legislation comparable to benefits given under the war pensions and allowances plans.
I believe the hon. member has adopted, by his argument, a course of proceeding by legislation comparable to military pensions; but I suggest, sir, that the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act in its original purpose, in its framework, in its philosophy, in the way it was set out, was analogous-parallel, if you like-to the workmen's compensation acts of the various provinces. I do not say this is fatal to his bill. I would not argue that at all. But I think it should be at least known to the house that the apparent original purpose of the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act when it was passed by this parliament was to set up legislation comparable to workmen's compensation. I suggest, sir, from my knowledge-and I admit it is imperfect-that the provincial workmen's compensation acts do not contain provisions similar to the one presented to us in Bill No. C-25. Perhaps I am wrong in that, but that is my understanding from information given to me.
May I suggest a way that this problem, if it can be treated as a problem, should be solved. I think we all recognize the need for some help for the orphan class mentioned in the bill of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. It seems to me that to make our legislation all of a piece this is the sort of thing where the federal Department of Labour and the provincial departments of labour could work out a common philosophy for both workmen's compensation and the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act.
I now come to another point, Mr. Speaker. What are the rights or privileges with respect to orphan children as they now exist under the present act? First, a payment of $35 per month may be made to them until they reach the age of 18. Second, where it seems desirable to continue the existing household a suitable person acts as foster mother in keeping up the household and maintaining and taking care of these orphans entitled to compensation. That duty must be carried out in a manner satisfactory to the board. Under these circumstances the foster mother I have mentioned would be entitled to receive the same monthly payment for herself to a total of $75 per month, and the children $25 a month, as if she were the


widow of the deceased. Under the amendment presented to us by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo the bill would widen the discretion of the merchant seamen compensation board and make an allowance to a person who undertakes the care and main-tainance of orphans of merchant seamen who are entitled to compensation under this act.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) raised the question of the phrase "existing household". I understand there is no precise definition under the act we are considering as to the exact meaning of "existing household". However, apparently it means people living together as a unit under the same roof. As my hon. friend for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) points out to me, it does not mean the existing dwelling as a residence, but it is the family kept intact as a unit in the place where that is done. The hon. member by his amendment proposes that there be no requirement or prior condition that the existing household be continued, if I understand him correctly. He pointed out the example of an orphan in his riding who would, if the act were changed, receive a much greater benefit by being placed in a much better home and in the care of a person who would be able to do much more for him.
The amendment only requires that foster mothers maintain or care for such orphans or orphan. The keeping up of a domestic establishment is no longer a requirement. I asked the hon. member how many people would be involved if this amendment were to carry and I believe he gave the answer that 100 or more would be involved in his own province, and he projected that to hundreds in the maritime or Atlantic provinces of Canada. I am not sure if I understood him correctly as meaning this would be the total number of people who were now deprived of advantages under the act, advantages which they would otherwise receive. In any event, I find myself in sympathy with the bill more from the standpoint of heart or emotion than from reaching a conclusion on an intellectual basis because, as I pointed out earlier, the purpose of the act when originally set up was to parallel the function of the workmen's compensation boards in the various provinces and not, as the hon. member has said this afternoon, to parallel the provisions of the Pension Act. But whether that is a defect or not, I think the bill is worthy of our consideration and support.

speechtext:
I should like to enter this debate briefly. I find myself in the rare position of agreeing completely with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the hon. member for Humber-St. George's,

and I find myself in almost complete disagreement with my colleagues on this side of the house, the hon. member for Peace River and some others who have spoken. I shall attempt to show the points of difference as I continue.
The point was well taken that the important thing to do in the case of orphan children is to try to keep the family together, if that is possible. However, we must realize that if there is only one child there is often no family left to keep together-there is only one child for whom the best possible future should be provided. At the other end of the scale, if there is a large number of children it might be impossible to keep a family of eight, ten or more children together. What could be more sensible than to keep children in a good home rather than grasp at the services of someone who might be completely unsatisfactory for the sake of $75-not a large amount these days, it is true, though it would be helpful in supplementing income from other sources. If it is possible to get two or three children into a good home, full payment should be made in such a case. I think that point was well taken. I do not think any penalty should be imposed because a child is taken under another roof. After all, we do want to provide the best possible home for the child.
I was interested in another phase of this debate in connection with the merchant seamen of this country. This is a maritime nation with a long coast line. We know that in two wars if it had not been for the gallant contribution of these men the tide of events might have turned out differently. Many lost their lives but, happily, many survived. I can think of one member of this house, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) who served for six years and has a gallant record of service in the merchant navy. I think anything we can do to make service in the merchant navy more attractive should be done. I think that is a principle of this bill, too. I know the hon. member who introduced the measure is most sincere about this. If a man can go to sea knowing that, should he lose his life, his wife and children will get the best possible care, that is most important to him.
A few moments ago the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave)-the taller member for Halifax, we sometimes call him-said, if I understood him correctly, that we should not try to make this legislation parallel to the provisions of the Pension Act. Here again, I find myself in disagreement with a colleague on this side of the house because I think those of us who serve on the veterans affairs committee and, indeed, most people in Canada, agree that Canadian pension legislation is second to none. If we could pattern the rest
Business of the House
of our legislation on the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act I think we should have a better country in which to live. A year ago the merchant seamen who served in wartime came under the War Veterans Allowance Act for the first time. Prior to that they had been provided for under certain parts of the veterans charter. It seems to me that this was a change which was long overdue.
Perhaps my hon. friend from Halifax did not read the sections of the Pension Act which are specially applicable. They are mentioned here in the explanatory notes on this bill where we are invited to compare subsections (9), (10) and (10a) of section 26 of the Pension Act as substituted by chapter 10 of the 196061 session. I should like to quote briefly from section 26:
(9)	On and after the death of the wife of a pensioner pensioned on account of disability, or the dissolution of her marriage, the additional pension for a married member of the forces may, in the discretion of the commission, be continued to him for so long as there is a minor child or there are minor children in respect of whom additional pension is being paid, if there exists a daughter or other person competent to assume and who does assume the household duties and care of the said child or children.
Then subsection 10 goes on to say:
(10)	On and after the death of a widow of a member of the forces who has been in receipt of a pension, the pension for the widow may, in the discretion of the commission, be continued for so long as there is a minor child or there are minor children to or in respect of whom a pension is being paid, to a daughter or other person competent to assume and who does assume the household duties and care of the other child or children; in such cases the pension payable for children shall continue.

speechtext: I wonder if the leader of the house could give us any information about what business the government proposes to bring before the house next week. In asking this I would draw the attention of the leader of the house to the fact that last night my hon. friend from Laurier pointed out that there was to have been a conference today- and I know he waited for it most of the day today-among the house leaders to effect co-operation with regard to business.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate gets exercised over these matters. A meeting of the leaders of the various parties was held yesterday at which certain conclusions were reached. I was then instructed to draft a proposed timetable for the coming week and submit it to the whips to transmit to their respective leaders. The

Business of the House
whips were asked to meet last night at 8.15 or 8.30 but none of them appeared, and until I get word from the whips as to whether there are modifications desired in this program there is not much purpose in attempting to have further consultations.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: On a question of privilege, last night we were asked, as whips, to meet. I informed the government whip that this matter was to be dealt with by the house leaders of each party-that the whips had nothing to do with it. They were told immediately that it was to be taken up with the house leaders of each party, not with the whips. The minister is not going to get away with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not trying to get away with anything. If there is a lack of communication between the parties, that is not my responsibility.

On a question of privilege, it is a well known fact that when my hon. friend the hon. member for Laurier is not here I act on his behalf. The hon. member for Laurier was told by the leader of our party after the meeting with the Prime Minister yesterday that the house leaders had been instructed to meet at the call of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, and the hon. member for Laurier has been waiting since that time until about an hour ago to attend that meeting. To the best of my knowledge that meeting has not been called. My hon. friend has had to go away and he has instructed me to attend in his place if it is called. All this shows to me that the government does not want co-operation and that it does not want to get on with its business.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I am not taking instructions from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate or from any one other than the Prime Minister.
Speak up.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I said I am not taking instructions from anyone in this house with the exception of the Prime Minister, and I have told the house what my instructions were.
On Monday we shall continue with the discussion of the bill dealing with the Atlantic development board which we were on today, and we shall follow that with a discussion of the national economic development board bill which is now in second reading. I hope the leaders of the various parties will examine the proposed timetable which has been typed out and distributed. If there are suggestions to be made, on Monday we could consider the matter.
I would like, also, on Monday, to ask the house to give consideration at five o'clock as

the first item during that period to the bill standing in the name of hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) dealing with a proposal concerning the handling of divorce in parliament.

I wonder if I might ask the leader of the house whether any proposal has been made in an informal way about the last point which the hon. gentleman raised because, normally, motions, not bills are taken on Mondays. I am not offering any objection, but has any proposal been made to the leaders of the other parties about this?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: This matter was discussed at a meeting of the leaders in the Prime Minister's office and I asked the hon. member for Marquette to make an investigation himself to see if this would be agreeable to the various parties.

May I make a suggestion with regard to the business of the house. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has suggested that the program which has been given to each of the political leaders be reviewed. I just wish to point out that as to the meeting which was held yesterday with the Prime Minister I think there has been some misunderstanding, and I think we ought not to discontinue the arrangements which were suggested the other day. There may be some misunderstanding as to what the terms were. Certainly my understanding was that the whips and the house leaders would meet. I would suggest that this idea be carried forward. I do not think we should be asked just to accept the list of legislation sent to us by a representative of the government. I think the whips and the house leaders should review the matter. Then the meeting which the Prime Minister said would be held with the leaders of the various parties could then be proceeded with.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That throws some more light on the matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Without creating a precedent, I think there is perhaps under the circumstances some justification for members from each of the parties speaking. However, this is not a rule of conduct, namely that on the discussion of business we get representatives of all the parties participating. It is usually the opposition house leader who asks the house leader what the business is to be. In the circumstances, however, if there is some point to be clarified, I will hear the hon. member for Red Deer.

I should just like to verify what was said by the hon. member for

Burnaby-Coquitlam. This was the arrangement that I understood was to be followed. I understood that when the whips and the house leaders got together, then the leaders would again meet to verify the procedure we would follow. I mention this only because we certainly wish to go ahead with legislation. This was the purpose of our meeting
Business of the House and this is what we ought to be doing. I would also mention that it was agreed the other day that we go ahead with this divorce question; and it was our plan that it come up as soon as possible, if there is agreement.
